title: Hidden fees to watch for in restaurant software
description: Restaurant software hidden fees can show up in setup, monthly minimums, per-order charges, and forwarding costs. Check these before you buy.
question: What hidden fees should I look for in restaurant software pricing?
answer: Look for setup fees, monthly minimums, per-order charges, per-minute charges, contract terms, and add-on fees for extra locations, forwarding, or support. For phone tools, also ask whether test calls, menu updates, and unanswered calls cost extra. The safest pricing is the one you can map to real orders and real call volume.
summary: You’ll learn how to spot hidden software fees and compare pricing with real restaurant numbers.
intro:
Restaurant software hidden fees usually show up in the places owners do not check first: setup, minimums, add-ons, and usage charges. The cleanest way to compare vendors is to turn every price into a simple monthly number based on your own call volume.

For a pizza shop, deli, or family restaurant, that matters fast. A cheap-looking plan can cost more than it sounds once orders start coming in, while a pay-per-order model like ROAL can be easier to tie to actual tickets instead of guesses.

sections.h2: What fees hide behind a low monthly price?
sections.body:
A low sticker price often leaves out the parts that cost you later. When you compare restaurant software, ask what is included in the base price and what is billed separately.

Here is a simple checklist you can use on the phone or in an email:
- Setup fee or onboarding fee
- Per-location fee
- Per-order fee
- Per-minute fee
- Extra charge for forwarding calls
- Charge for text messages, recordings, or transcripts
- Fee for support, training, or menu changes
- Contract minimum or cancellation fee

A quick script helps: "Can you tell me the total monthly cost for one location, with no setup fee, no minimum, and no extra charge for normal order volume?" That one question forces a real answer. If they hesitate, ask them to put the pricing in writing. ROAL keeps things simpler here: no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. It is $0.90 per completed phone order, billed monthly.

sections.h2: How do per-order, per-minute, and monthly plans compare?
sections.body:
Different pricing models can look cheap until you run the math. The right one depends on how many calls you get and how many actually become orders.

Use this example and swap in your own numbers:
- Say your shop gets 200 call attempts in a month
- Say 80 of those become completed orders
- Say your average order is $28

Now compare the common models:

| Pricing model | How it charges | What to watch |
|---|---|---|
| Monthly plan | Fixed fee every month | You pay even when volume is slow |
| Per-minute plan | Billed by call time | Longer menu questions cost more |
| Per-call plan | Billed for each call | Can charge for junk calls and questions |
| Per-order plan | Billed only for completed orders | Check what counts as "completed" |

With a per-order model like ROAL, 80 completed orders would cost $72 at $0.90 each. That does not include the rest of the calls, because questions and test calls are free. A monthly plan at $199 would cost more that month even if your order count stayed the same. Plug in your own volume and compare the real total, not the headline price. For a deeper pricing breakdown, see [How much does AI phone answering cost a restaurant?](/blog/ai-phone-answering-cost-restaurant).

sections.h2: What should I ask about setup, onboarding, and support fees?
sections.body:
Setup fees are one of the easiest hidden costs to miss. Some products charge to build your account, import your menu, train the system, or launch your first location. Others charge again if you add a second location or update the menu in a special way.

Before you sign anything, ask these exact questions:
1. Is setup included?
2. Is menu import included?
3. Are updates to hours, prices, and FAQs included?
4. Is support included, or is there a paid support tier?
5. If I add a second location, does pricing change?

A restaurant example: if one vendor charges a $299 setup fee and $149 per month, that is $1,087 in the first six months before you count usage. If another vendor charges no setup fee and only bills for completed orders, the early cost can be much lower during slower weeks. ROAL lets owners paste a website, Google Maps link, or restaurant name at /try, read public menu and hours data, and test-call the host right in the browser with no sign-up needed. That makes it easier to check the fit before you commit. You can also upload a menu in any format.

sections.h2: Where do delivery app and forwarding costs sneak in?
sections.body:
Hidden fees are not only inside software. They also show up in the way calls and orders move through your operation. Delivery apps commonly charge restaurants roughly 15-30% commission per order, so a phone order that bypasses those commissions can matter a lot.

If you forward calls to a new phone line, make sure your carrier or phone system does not add surprises. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 forwards all calls and *73 turns it off. On some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off. Busy and unanswered forwarding can use different codes. Verizon Wireless uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call.

Use this quick check:
- Ask whether forwarded calls count as normal airtime
- Ask whether your existing number stays active
- Ask whether you pay extra for each location line
- Ask whether you can turn forwarding off any time

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and the restaurant keeps its own number. You can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered.

sections.h2: How do I compare hidden fees with real restaurant numbers?
sections.body:
The easiest way to avoid surprises is to compare pricing using one normal month from your shop. Use your own numbers, not vendor guesses.

Try this worksheet:
- Average order value: $____
- Completed phone orders per month: ____
- Monthly plan price: $____
- Setup fee: $____
- Extra support or menu update fee: $____
- Forwarding or phone-system fee: $____

Now calculate the first-month total:
1. Monthly plan price
2. Plus setup fee
3. Plus any add-ons
4. Plus any forwarding charges
5. Divide by completed orders

Example: say you get 60 completed phone orders and a vendor charges $149 per month plus a $250 setup fee. Your first month is $399, or about $6.65 per completed order before any other fees. If another option charges $0.90 per completed order, the same 60 orders would cost $54. That is the kind of comparison owners should make. If you want a simple worksheet, [the AI phone host cost calculator](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator) can help you plug in your own numbers.

sections.h2: What should I check before I sign a contract?
sections.body:
A contract can hide costs that do not show up on the landing page. Read the boring parts. That is where the bill usually lives.

Before you sign, check for these items:
- Minimum term or auto-renewal
- Cancellation fee
- Price increase after the intro period
- Limit on included locations
- Extra charges for support, transcripts, or recordings
- Rules about forwarding, call volume, or menu changes

A simple restaurant-owner question works well: "If I cancel after two months, what do I owe, and what exact charges can still show up?" Ask for the answer in plain language. If you need a comparison point, ROAL is billed monthly and has no contract. It also gives you call history with transcripts and recordings, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus in the dashboard. That way, the software bill is easier to match to what it actually did for the restaurant.

sections.h2: How can I keep my phone software bill predictable?
sections.body:
Predictable pricing matters more than flashy features when you are busy on the line. The goal is to know what the bill will look like before the month ends.

A simple operating routine helps:
1. Write down your average completed phone orders per week.
2. Check whether questions, test calls, and busy-time calls are free.
3. Confirm whether updates to hours and menu items are included.
4. Review the bill after the first month and compare it with the quote.
5. Keep one person responsible for tracking changes.

If you use ROAL, the host can take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, answer hours and address questions, speak the caller’s language, and hand trickier calls to staff with a summary. It does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment stays where your restaurant already handles it. If you want to see the setup path, [Build a free test host](/try) from your website or Google Maps link and test-call it before you decide. That is often the fastest way to see whether the pricing fits the way your shop really runs.

takeaways: Ask for the full monthly cost, not just the headline price.
Compare pricing using completed orders, not guesses.
Watch for setup fees, minimums, and add-ons.
Confirm forwarding rules with your carrier before you rely on them.
Use your own restaurant numbers to judge whether the pricing is predictable.

faq.q: What hidden fees should I ask about in restaurant software?
faq.a: Ask about setup fees, monthly minimums, per-order charges, per-minute charges, cancellation fees, support fees, and extra location fees. Also ask whether menu updates, recordings, transcripts, and call forwarding cost extra. The total matters more than the headline price.

faq.q: Is a monthly fee or per-order pricing better for a restaurant?
faq.a: It depends on volume. A monthly fee can make sense if your call volume is steady and the plan is truly all-in, but it can feel expensive during slower months. Per-order pricing is easier to match to actual tickets because you pay when completed orders happen.

faq.q: Do restaurant phone tools charge for test calls and questions?
faq.a: Some do, and that can add up if you are testing or getting a lot of menu questions. ROAL includes unlimited free calls, questions, and test calls, while billing only for completed phone orders. Always confirm what counts as billable before you buy.

faq.q: How do I know if call forwarding will cost extra?
faq.a: Ask your carrier or phone system directly, because codes and fees vary by plan. On many systems, forwarding can be set in the phone portal or by dialing a code, but your carrier may still charge normal airtime or forwarding-related fees. Test with one real call before you turn it on fully.
